Bordered cells highlight attention heads with statistically significant causal indirect effects (CIEs). 4.1 Methods We used activation patching to identify the attention heads that are functionally relevant for inference ( Todd et al., 2024 ; Yang et al., 2025 ) . Following the procedure in Section 3.1 , we constructed three corruption conditions s ~ \tilde{s} including description, label, and query corruption. Let 𝐚 ℓ , k ∈ ℝ d \mathbf{a}_{\ell,k}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} represent the output of the k th k^{\textrm{th}} attention head at layer ℓ \ell , projected into the residual stream. For each corrupted input, we intervened by replacing the corrupted head output 𝐚 ℓ , k corr \mathbf{a}_{\ell,k}^{\text{corr}} with its counterpart from the clean run 𝐚 ℓ , k clean \mathbf{a}_{\ell,k}^{\text{clean}} . The causal effect of this intervention was then measured via the causal indirect effect (CIE). We performed a permutation test to control the family-wise error rate and retained only heads with statistically significant effects ( p < 0.05 p<0.05 ; Appendix B.6 ). We then probed the attention patterns of the identified heads to characterize what contextual information they integrate. For each head, we aggregated attention mass across five token spans: (i) demonstration descriptions, (ii) mapping delimiters (e.g., “ ⇒ \Rightarrow ”), (iii) demonstration labels, (iv) query tokens, and (v) the final prompt delimiter preceding the prediction. This allows us to localize the specific contextual information the head preferentially attends to during inference. Finally, to assess the contribution of the identified heads to the shared conceptual subspace, we analyzed both the magnitude and directional consistency of their updates. Let 𝐖 ℓ ∈ ℝ d × r \mathbf{W}_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times r} denote the GCCA-derived projection matrix for layer ℓ \ell , and 𝐘 ℓ = 𝐗 ℓ ​ 𝐖 ℓ ∈ ℝ n × r \mathbf{Y}_{\ell}=\mathbf{X}_{\ell}\mathbf{W}_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r} be the projected hidden states of n n concepts. For a head k k at layer ℓ \ell with stacked outputs 𝐀 ℓ , k ∈ ℝ n × d \mathbf{A}_{\ell,k}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d} , we define the head-induced subspace update as: Δ ​ 𝐘 ℓ , k := 𝐀 ℓ , k ​ 𝐖 ℓ ∈ ℝ n × r \Delta\mathbf{Y}_{\ell,k}:=\mathbf{A}_{\ell,k}\mathbf{W}_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r} . To characterize the nature of these updates, we computed two complementary metrics: (i) contribution strength ( α ℓ , k \alpha_{\ell,k} ) and (ii) directional alignment ( align ℓ , k \text{align}_{\ell,k} ). Contribution strength measures the magnitude of the head’s update relative to the total subspace energy: α ℓ , k = ‖ Δ ​ 𝐘 ℓ , k ‖ F 2 ‖ 𝐘 ℓ , k ‖ F 2 \alpha_{\ell,k}=\frac{\|\Delta\!\mathbf{Y}_{\ell,k}\|_{F}^{2}}{\|\mathbf{Y}_{\ell,k}\|_{F}^{2}} , and directional alignment quantifies the geometric coherence between the head’s update and the target subspace representation by their cosine similarity: align ℓ , k = ⟨ Δ ​ 𝐘 ℓ , k , 𝐘 ℓ , k ⟩ ‖ Δ ​ 𝐘 ℓ , k ‖ F ​ ‖ 𝐘 ℓ , k ‖ F \textrm{align}_{\ell,k}=\frac{\left\langle\Delta\!\mathbf{Y}_{\ell,k},\mathbf{Y}_{\ell,k}\right\rangle}{\|\Delta\!\mathbf{Y}_{\ell,k}\|_{F}\|\mathbf{Y}_{\ell,k}\|_{F}} , where ⟨ ⋅ , ⋅ ⟩ \left\langle\cdot,\cdot\right\rangle denotes the Frobenius inner product. For heads located in layers ℓ \ell prior to the first available subspace basis at layer ℓ ∗ \ell^{\ast} , we calculated α ℓ , k \alpha_{\ell,k} and align ℓ , k \textrm{align}_{\ell,k} relative to 𝐖 ℓ ∗ \mathbf{W}_{\ell^{\ast}} . This approach is motivated by the hypothesis that information written to the residual stream can persist and remain linearly accessible to subsequent layers. 4.2 Results Activation patching across corruption conditions reveals a progression of information integration (Figures 4 – 5 ; Appendix Figure 12 a–c). Under demonstration corruptions (descriptions and labels), statistically significant heads were concentrated in the early-to-middle layers (17–40), coinciding with the depth at which the shared conceptual subspace emerged and began to causally mediate contextual information (around layers 36–40; Section 3.2 ). The substantial overlap between heads identified under description and label corruptions suggests a joint mechanism that integrates these components to construct an abstract conceptual subspace, with description corruption yielding stronger CIEs (Appendix Figure 12 a–c), likely due to its role in contextualizing the query ( Bakalova et al., 2025 ) . In contrast, query corruption implicated a later set of heads spanning the middle to late layers, mirroring our observation that query information is mediated by the conceptual subspace over an extended stage of processing. Mid-layer heads (approximately 33–42) likely support query-related computations within the subspace, whereas the final-layer heads (79–80) may implement a readout stage that converts subspace representations into surface-form token predictions. Attention mass attribution reveals a functional shift from demonstration-centric to query-centric processing (Figure 4 ). Heads identified under demonstration corruptions and located before layer 38 allocated most attention to contextual descriptions, delimiters, and labels, consistent with a role in extracting and integrating demonstration-related cues to construct the subspace. Beyond roughly layer 40, these heads shifted attention toward the query and the final prompt delimiter, signaling a transition from subspace construction to query-conditioned inference. Heads identified under query corruption exhibited heavy attention to query tokens, while the final-layer heads attended predominantly to the last delimiter to facilitate next-token prediction. The identified heads were also geometrically aligned with the conceptual subspace (Figure 5 ). Significant heads in early-to-middle layers exhibited both higher contribution strength ( α \alpha ) and greater directional alignment ( align ) compared to non-significant heads. While contribution strength decreased in later layers, directional alignment remained high, suggesting that late-layer computations stay coordinated with the already-established subspace. Together, these results suggest a two-stage process: (i) Construction, where early-to-middle layers integrate demonstration-derived cues to build and stabilize the conceptual subspace; and (ii) Utilization, where subsequent layers operate within this structured subspace to support inference and produce the final prediction. Results from other LLMs support the generality of our findings (Appendix C.3 ). 5 Related Work The in-context learning capacity of LLMs ( Brown et al., 2020 ; Lampinen et al., 2024b ) has been studied extensively from both theoretical and empirical perspectives. Theoretically, in-context learning has been framed as approximate Bayesian inference ( Xie et al., 2022 ; Hahn and Goyal, 2023 ; Wies et al., 2023 ) or as a form of meta-learning emerging from next-token prediction ( Akyürek et al., 2023 ; Chan et al., 2022 ; Mahankali et al., 2024 ) . Empirically, research has investigated how various contextual factors can shape model behavior and generalization ( Min et al., 2022 ) . Hybrid in-context and in-weight learning in neural networks has been shown to capture aspects of human learning and generalization ( Russin et al., 2025 ; Lake and Baroni, 2023 ) . While these lines of work characterize what problems in-context learning can solve, the internal machinery that implement these computations remains a subject of active debate. Mechanistic interpretability seeks to decompose LLM computation into interpretable components and circuits ( Elhage et al., 2021 ; Meng et al., 2022 ; Bakalova et al., 2025 ; Cho et al., 2025 ) . A growing body of work has identified mechanisms supporting abstract or symbolic-like operations during in-context learning ( Olsson et al., 2022 ; Hendel et al., 2023 ; Todd et al., 2024 ; Feng and Steinhardt, 2024 ; Feucht et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2025 ) . However, much of this evidence comes from relatively simple, synthetic, or tightly controlled settings. Our results complement this literature by moving beyond individual attention heads to identify an abstract conceptual subspace formed in the residual stream. Crucially, we show that this subspace is not merely a byproduct but is causally engaged during inference on real-world knowledge. Our work also builds on previous work probing the internal representations learned by LLMs. Evidence suggests that these models encode substantial conceptual knowledge ( Forbes et al., 2019 ; Xu et al., 2025 ) and can dynamically form representations of world state ( Gurnee and Tegmark, 2024 ; Li et al., 2023 ; Park et al., 2025 ) . Despite this progress, it remains unclear whether and how such structured representations are formed and used during inference. We bridge this gap by linking representational structure to causal mechanisms, demonstrating how LLMs construct and leverage a conceptual subspace to perform in-context inference. 6 Discussion In this work, we identify an emergent representational structure that bridges raw contextual input and abstract inference. Our results show how LLMs construct a dedicated conceptual subspace that abstracts away surface-level details while organizing concepts into a coherent relational structure. This structure persists across contexts and is functionally engaged during inference. These findings inform ongoing debates about the capacity of LLMs for genuine inference: despite being trained solely for next-token prediction, they can learn internal representational substrates that approximate abstract, structured inference rather than relying exclusively on superficial heuristics. Prior work suggests that middle layers contain substantial structured knowledge and encode meaningful aspects of world state ( Skean et al., 2025 ; Park et al., 2025 ) . Our results complement this view by showing how contextual information and stored knowledge are integrated across middle to late layers to form a coherent conceptual structure that later computations can exploit for task-specific inference. A natural next step is to trace more concretely how information encoded in the conceptual subspace is transformed into the target output, and whether analogous substrates support broader forms of reasoning. More generally, connecting such mechanisms to theories of concepts can help clarify how structured inference and reasoning can emerge in both humans and machines ( Piantadosi et al., 2024 ; Johnson-Laird, 2010 ) . While the conceptual subspace is sufficient and causally central to inference, ablation results also reveal redundancy and compensatory pathways. This raises the possibility that models implement partially overlapping routes to the same behavioral outcome, an important consideration for mechanistic claims and for connecting distributed computation to the symbolic or structured procedures it can approximate. Moreover, our results on smaller models suggest that clean reliance on an abstract conceptual subspace is emergent and scale-dependent. Future work could characterize when models learn to construct and use such an abstract subspace versus alternative pathways, and whether these routes differ in robustness, sample efficiency, or generalization profile. Finally, our results highlight that the mechanisms supporting inference—and the functional roles of model components—shift systematically as contextual evidence accumulates. Understanding how internal processing changes across contexts, and how post-training interventions alter models’ dependence on contextual cues, is an important direction both for theory-building and for predicting how models will generalize across scenarios, with direct implications for AI safety and reliability. Appendix A Data, Code, and Materials Availability This work uses publicly available datasets and materials ( Hebart et al., 2019 ) . Code to reproduce all experiments will be released at https://github.com/ningyuxu/llm_structured_icl . Appendix B Supplementary Methods B.1 Models Our experiments focus on base models—LLMs pretrained solely with next-token prediction, without any post-training or instruction tuning. Table 1 lists the set of open-source LLMs we used. We report results for Llama-3.1 70B in the main paper, as it is the largest model evaluated and achieved the strongest behavioral performance on the reverse dictionary task, making it a suitable representative for illustrating the emergence of the conceptual subspace. Results for the remaining models are provided in the Appendix. B.2 Data Our experiments employ data from the THINGS database ( Hebart et al., 2019 ) (available at https://osf.io/jum2f/ ), which contains 1,854 concrete, nameable object concepts selected to be representative of everyday objects commonly used in American English. Each concept is paired with its WordNet synset ID, definitional descriptions, and multiple associated images, providing a suitable testbed for analyzing conceptual representations derived from descriptions. To probe in-context concept inference in LLMs, we randomly designated 20% of the concepts as a training set, from which N N description–word pairs were sampled to form the demonstrations. The remaining concepts were used as the test set. For each experimental condition, we evaluated models across five independent runs, each using a distinct random sample of N N demonstrations. B.3 Generalized Canonical Correlation Analysis (GCCA) GCCA Eigenvalue Formulation. We employed GCCA to identify a low-dimensional subspace that is shared across model layers. Let 𝐗 ℓ ∈ ℝ n × d \mathbf{X}_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d} denote the matrix of hidden states at layer ℓ \ell , where each row 𝐗 ℓ [ i , : ] = 𝐡 ℓ , i \mathbf{X}_{\ell}[i,:]=\mathbf{h}_{\ell,i} corresponds to the representation of the i th i^{\textrm{th}} query concept, n n is the number of query concepts, and d d is the hidden dimensionality of the model. Unless otherwise stated, we set the ridge regularization parameter to λ = 0.01 \lambda=0.01 for numerical stability. The eigenvectors of 𝐒 \mathbf{S} corresponding to its largest eigenvalues define directions that exhibit strong alignment across layers, and thus constitute the shared subspace. Rank Selection via Permutation Testing. To determine the dimensionality r ^ \hat{r} of the conceptual subspace shared across layers, we employed a non-parametric permutation test. The null hypothesis is that any apparent alignment across layers arises from chance correlations rather than shared structure. Specifically, for each layer ℓ \ell , we independently applied a random permutation π ℓ \pi_{\ell} to the rows of 𝐗 ℓ \mathbf{X}_{\ell} , yielding a permuted matrix 𝐗 ℓ π \mathbf{X}_{\ell}^{\pi} . This procedure destroys the correspondence between representations of the same query concept across layers, while preserving the marginal covariance structure within each layer. We repeated this permutation procedure M = 500 M=500 times. For each permutation, we computed the eigenvalue spectrum { λ i π } \{\lambda_{i}^{\pi}\} of the corresponding GCCA operator 𝐒 π \mathbf{S}^{\pi} . For each component index i i , we defined a significance threshold q i q_{i} as the ( 1 − α ) (1-\alpha) quantile of the null distribution of λ i π \lambda_{i}^{\pi} , with α = 0.05 \alpha=0.05 . The effective rank r ^ \hat{r} of the shared subspace was then determined as the number of eigenvalues from the original (unpermuted) data whose magnitude exceeded the corresponding null threshold: r ^ = ∑ i = 1 r max 𝕀 ⁡ ( λ i > q i ) . \hat{r}=\sum_{i=1}^{r_{\max}}\mathbb{I}\!\left(\lambda_{i}>q_{i}\right). Subspace Overlap via Principal Angles. To compare subspaces derived under different contexts, we assessed the overlap between the column spaces of the corresponding projection matrices 𝐖 ℓ c \mathbf{W}_{\ell}^{c} , where c c indexes the set of demonstrations provided in context. For each 𝐖 ℓ c \mathbf{W}_{\ell}^{c} , we obtained an orthonormal basis 𝐔 ℓ c \mathbf{U}_{\ell}^{c} via QR decomposition. Given two sets of demonstrations c c and c ′ c^{\prime} , we computed the principal angles { θ i } i = 1 r \{\theta_{i}\}_{i=1}^{r} between the subspaces spanned by 𝐔 ℓ c \mathbf{U}_{\ell}^{c} and 𝐔 ℓ c ′ \mathbf{U}_{\ell}^{c^{\prime}} . Subspace overlap is quantified as the mean squared cosine of these angles: 1 r ​ ∑ i = 1 r cos 2 ⁡ θ i \frac{1}{r}\sum_{i=1}^{r}\cos^{2}\theta_{i} . This metric measures whether different contexts induce similar linear subspaces within the model’s hidden-state space. Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA). We employed representational similarity analysis (RSA) to compare the relational structure of concepts encoded within different conceptual subspaces. RSA is nonparametric and has been widely adopted to measure alignment between representation spaces based on their similarity structure. For each context (prompt) s s and layer ℓ \ell , we computed a representational dissimilarity matrix (RDM) 𝐃 ℓ c ∈ ℝ n × n \mathbf{D}_{\ell}^{c}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} from the projected representations 𝐘 ℓ c = 𝐗 ℓ c ​ 𝐖 ℓ c \mathbf{Y}_{\ell}^{c}=\mathbf{X}_{\ell}^{c}\mathbf{W}_{\ell}^{c} , where each entry 𝐃 ℓ , i ​ j c = 1 − cos ( 𝐘 ℓ , i , : c , 𝐘 ℓ , j , : c ) \mathbf{D}_{\ell,ij}^{c}=1-\cos\!\left(\mathbf{Y}_{\ell,i,:}^{c},\mathbf{Y}_{\ell,j,:}^{c}\right) measures the dissimilarity between concepts i i and j j . RSA alignment between representations derived under contexts s s and s ′ s^{\prime} is then measured by the Spearman’s rank correlation between the upper-triangular entries of 𝐃 ℓ c \mathbf{D}_{\ell}^{c} and 𝐃 ℓ c ′ \mathbf{D}_{\ell}^{c^{\prime}} . B.5 Behavioral Evaluation We evaluated model performance in concept inference by truncating each generation at the first newline character (“\n”) and checking whether the resulting output exactly matched the target word or any of its listed synonyms in the THINGS database. We used greedy decoding for all models to ensure a consistent and controlled comparison across model sizes and families. B.6 Causal Mediation Analysis Causal Indirect Effect and Causal Mediation Score. We employed log probabilities to measure the causal effect of interventions on the model’s predictions. This score represents the change in the log probability difference between the source-related token y q a y_{q_{a}} and the target-correct token y q b y_{q_{b}} after the intervention: CMA \displaystyle\mathrm{CMA} = ( log ⁡ f ℳ ​ ( c j , s q b ∣ 𝐡 ℓ patch ) ​ [ y q a ] − log ⁡ f ℳ ​ ( c j , s q b ∣ 𝐡 ℓ patch ) ​ [ y q b ] ) \displaystyle=\left(\log f_{\mathcal{M}}\!\left(c_{j},s_{q_{b}}\mid\mathbf{h}_{\ell}^{\textrm{patch}}\right)\left[y_{q_{a}}\right]-\log f_{\mathcal{M}}\!\left(c_{j},s_{q_{b}}\mid\mathbf{h}_{\ell}^{\textrm{patch}}\right)\left[y_{q_{b}}\right]\right) (8) − ( log ⁡ f ℳ ​ ( c j , s q b ) ​ [ y q a ] − log ⁡ f ℳ ​ ( c j , s q b ) ​ [ y q b ] ) . \displaystyle-\left(\log f_{\mathcal{M}}\!\left(c_{j},s_{q_{b}}\right)\left[y_{q_{a}}\right]-\log f_{\mathcal{M}}\!\left(c_{j},s_{q_{b}}\right)\left[y_{q_{b}}\right]\right). We preferred log probabilities over raw logits because logits are unconstrained outputs that can vary significantly in scale across different conditions. Log probabilities are normalized via the softmax function, ensuring that the metrics reflect the model’s relative confidence in its predictions. This makes them a more stable and interpretable objective for quantifying the functional impact of interventions across varying contexts. Identification of Significant Attention Heads via Permutation Testing. To identify the attention heads that are functionally relevant for inference in LLMs, we performed statistical tests to determine which heads exhibit statistically significant causal effects. We employed a non-parametric permutation test to control the family-wise error rate (FWER) at α = 0.05 \alpha=0.05 , with the null hypothesis assuming the absence of any real causal effects. For each permutation, we disrupted the relationship between specific heads and the model’s output by applying random sign-flipping to the observed causal indirect effects (CIEs). Specifically, each CIE was multiplied by a value sampled uniformly from { − 1 , 1 } \{-1,1\} , and this procedure was repeated 5,000 times. To account for multiple comparisons, we constructed a null distribution based on the maximum CIE observed for each permutation. The significance threshold was then defined as the ( 1 − α ) (1-\alpha) -quantile of this empirical null distribution. Attention heads were classified as significant if their observed CIE exceeded this threshold. We restricted our analysis to these significant heads to focus on those contributing constructively to the in-context concept inference task. Layer-wise SVD showed that early layers exhibited relatively low cross-layer overlap, whereas middle-to-late layers maintained high inter-layer overlap. This transition coincided with a sharp increase in the number of principal components required to explain 95% of the variance (Figures 7 a–b,f–g; 8 a–b,f–g,k–l), suggesting the integration of contextual information into a higher-dimensional subspace. Subspaces identified via GCCA demonstrated near-unity GCCA alignment scores and RSA values across layers. Increasing the number of demonstrations from 1 to 24 led to progressively stronger cross-context alignment of the internal subspace structure, with diminishing gains beyond this threshold (Figures 7 d–e,i–j; 8 d–e,i–j,n–o). These trends were consistent across model families, though the relative depth at which the shared subspace emerges varied; for example, Qwen2.5 models manifested the shared subspaces at relatively later layers than Llama-3 and Llama-3.1 variants. Collectively, these results suggest that LLMs construct a conceptual subspace during inference that persists across middle to late layers. While larger models (e.g., Llama-3.1 70B) required higher-dimensional layer-wise subspaces to capture 95% of the variance (Figure 2 b), permutation testing identified fewer significant dimensions for GCCA analyses across layers (Table 1 ). Furthermore, these subspaces exhibited stronger cross-context alignment compared to smaller models. These findings indicate that increased model scale and compute support the formation of richer and more stable relational structures, which are encoded in a more coherent and compressed manner, revealing systematic differences in how LLMs organize internal computations during inference. C.2 Analyzing the Causal Role of Conceptual Subspaces in Inference across Models Besides Llama-3.1 70B, we applied the same set of targeted causal interventions to other LLMs; the corresponding results are shown in Figures 9 – 11 . Across models, we observed trends broadly consistent with those reported for Llama-3.1 70B, although the extent to which inference is mediated by the conceptual subspace varied across models. Specifically, activation patching under corrupted demonstrations and queries (Figures 9 a–c,g–i; 10 a–c,g–i) showed that demonstration-derived contextual information was primarily mediated by the conceptual subspace at mid-depth, where the subspace began to form, whereas query-related information was mediated at relatively later layers. While patching the conceptual subspace substantially recovered performance compared to random-subspace baselines, the recovery gap was narrower than that observed in Llama-3.1 70B. This suggests that, in these smaller models, task-relevant information may be represented in a more distributed manner, with weaker reliance on a localized, dominant conceptual subspace. Subspace ablation and isolation experiments (Figures 9 d–e,j–k; 10 d–e,j–k) revealed patterns similar to those in Llama-3.1 70B. Ablating the conceptual subspace consistently disrupted inference and led to a clear performance drop relative to the random-subspace baselines, although performance did not collapse entirely, indicating partial redundancy or compensatory pathways. Conversely, isolating the subspace preserved near-original performance at middle layers, with degradation in later layers where computation likely shifted toward surface-form generation. As in Llama-3.1 70B, increasing the number of demonstrations attenuated ablation effects, while isolation continued to preserve performance deeper in the model, suggesting a progressively stronger reliance on the subspace as contextual information accumulates. Finally, cross-context transfer effects increased with the number of demonstrations and consistently exceeded the random-subspace baselines (Figures 9 f,l; 10 f,l), indicating that these models can construct relational structure that generalizes across contexts. However, the magnitude of this effect was notably reduced in smaller models. This trend was especially pronounced in Qwen2.5 3B (Figure 11 ), where random-subspace baselines often matched or exceeded the effects of the derived conceptual subspace across interventions. Together, these results suggest a transition in representational strategy: whereas larger models leverage well-defined, abstract conceptual subspaces to approximate in-context inference, smaller models rely more heavily on diffuse or non-subspace-specific representations. C.3 Analyzing Context Integration into Conceptual Subspaces across Models Across the LLMs we tested, activation patching across corruption conditions show a staged progression of information integration consistent with the patterns observed in Llama-3.1 70B. Heads with statistically significant effects under demonstration corruptions (descriptions and labels) clustered in early-to-middle layers for Llama-3.1 8B and Llama-3 8B (Figure 12 ), yet shifted toward middle-to-late layers in the Qwen2.5 models (Figure 13 ). These depth ranges aligned with the formation of the shared conceptual subspace and its causal mediation of contextual information (Sections C.1 – C.2 ). We also observed substantial overlap between heads identified under description and label corruptions, suggesting a shared mechanism for integrating demonstration-derived cues into the conceptual subspace. In larger models (Llama-3.1 70B and Qwen2.5 32B), description corruption typically implicated more heads and yielded larger causal indirect effects (CIEs) than label corruption. This likely reflects the role of descriptions in contextualizing the query ( Bakalova et al., 2025 ) , which appears more pronounced as model capacity increases. Conversely, query corruption consistently implicated a relatively later set of heads, mirroring our observation that query information is mediated by the conceptual subspace over a later stage of processing. These mid-to-late layer heads likely support query-conditioned computations given the established context, whereas final-layer heads may be engaged in a readout stage that maps internal representations to surface-form token predictions. Attention patterns further reveal a functional shift from demonstration-centric to query-centric processing (Figure 14 ). Heads identified under demonstration corruptions and located in relatively early layers allocated most attention to descriptions, delimiters, and labels, consistent with extracting and integrating demonstration cues to construct or update the subspace. In contrast, later-layer heads shifted attention toward the query and the final prompt delimiter, signaling a transition from subspace construction to query-conditioned inference. Heads identified under query corruption attended heavily to query tokens, while final-layer heads attended more strongly to the last delimiter, consistent with next-token prediction. The identified heads were also geometrically aligned with the conceptual subspace (Figures 15 – 16 ). Significant heads in early-to-middle layers of Llama-3 (or middle-to-late layers of Qwen2.5) exhibited higher contribution strength ( α \alpha ) and stronger directional alignment ( align ) than non-significant heads. While contribution strength generally decreased in later layers, directional alignment remained relatively high, suggesting that late-layer computations stay coordinated with an already-established subspace (Figure 15 ). Figure 16 further shows a qualitative difference in how heads interact with this subspace: heads identified under query corruption predominantly wrote coherently into the conceptual subspace (positive directional alignment), suggesting a role in using or stabilizing the subspace for prediction. In contrast, heads identified under demonstration corruption can exhibit substantial write strength ( α \alpha ) but weaker alignment, indicating a role in constructing or reconfiguring the subspace based on contextual evidence rather than simply amplifying existing directions. In larger models (Llama-3.1 70B and Qwen2.5 32B), we observed notable overlap among the heads identified across corruption conditions; these heads exhibited both high contribution strength and high alignment (Figure 16 a,d), indicating a core set of components that integrate relevant contextual information and directly drive model inference. In smaller models, causally relevant heads were more diffuse and can show weaker alignment or contribution strength relative to other heads (Figures 16 b–c,e–f; 15 g–i). Finally, individual heads in the larger models tended to have lower contribution strengths than those in smaller models, suggesting that computation is distributed across a broader ensemble of moderately weighted heads. Taken together, these findings support a two-stage account that generalizes across model families: (i) Construction, in which earlier layers integrate demonstration-derived cues to build and stabilize a conceptual subspace; and (ii) Utilization, in which later layers operate within this structured subspace to perform query-conditioned inference and generate the final prediction. Smaller models appear to rely less consistently on this mechanism, exhibiting more diffuse, non-subspace-specific strategies. Learn more × License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2602.07796v1 [cs.CL] 08 Feb 2026 \correspondingauthors { jli2947 , sharonli } @cs.wisc.edu \coderepo February 6, 2026 Thinking Makes LLM Agents Introverted: How Mandatory Thinking Can Backfire in User-Engaged Agents Jiatong Li Changdae Oh Hyeong Kyu Choi Jindong Wang Sharon Li Affiliation: University of Wisconsin–Madison Affiliation: William & Mary Abstract Eliciting reasoning has emerged as a powerful technique for improving the performance of large language models (LLMs) on complex tasks by inducing thinking. However, their effectiveness in realistic user-engaged agent scenarios remains unclear. In this paper, we conduct a comprehensive study on the effect of explicit thinking in user-engaged LLM agents. Our experiments span across seven models, three benchmarks, and two thinking instantiations, and we evaluate them through both a quantitative response taxonomy analysis and qualitative failure propagation case studies. Contrary to expectations, we find that mandatory thinking often backfires on agents in user-engaged settings, causing anomalous performance degradation across various LLMs. Our key finding reveals that thinking makes agents more “introverted” by shortening responses and reducing information disclosure to users, which weakens agent-user information exchange and leads to downstream task failures. Furthermore, we demonstrate that explicitly prompting for information disclosure reliably improves performance across diverse model families, suggesting that proactive transparency is a vital lever for agent optimization. Overall, our study suggests that information transparency awareness is a crucial yet underexplored perspective for the future design of reasoning agents in real-world scenarios. Our code is available at https://github.com/deeplearning-wisc/Thinking-Agent . 1 Introduction Figure 1: An overview of the research framework . Large language models (LLMs) have recently demonstrated remarkable gains on complex tasks by leveraging test-time reasoning ( Muennighoff et al., 2025 ) , often implemented through explicit thinking such as chain-of-thought prompting or dedicated reasoning modules. By explicitly encouraging models to think before acting, prior work has shown promising improvements on a wide range of closed-world benchmarks, including mathematical reasoning ( Sprague et al., 2025 ) and code generation ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) . As a result, “thinking before acting” has increasingly become a popular design in modern LLM-based agents ( Kim et al., 2025 ) . However, most real-world agents do not operate in closed, isolated manners. Instead, they are user-engaged ( Wang et al., 2024 ; Yao et al., 2025 ) : they interact with humans over multiple turns, operate under partial observability, and must actively communicate to elicit missing information, clarify intent, and guide users toward successful outcomes. In such settings, success depends not only on internal deliberation, but also on how agents communicate, disclose information, and guide users throughout the interaction. This raises a fundamental yet unexplored question: Is mandatory thinking still beneficial for LLM agents in realistic, user-engaged scenarios? In this paper, we present a systematic empirical study on the effect of thinking in user-engaged LLM agents. Across seven representative LLMs and established user-engaged benchmarks, we find a consistent and counterintuitive pattern: enabling thinking frequently degrades agent performance in multi-turn, user-facing environments. This effect holds across different model families, tasks, and two common instantiations of thinking, including Thinking-as-a-Function (TaaF), where reasoning is enforced as a mandatory pre-action function call in tool-using agents, and Thinking-as-a-Prefix (TaaP), where reasoning is elicited through ReAct-style prompt prefixes in text-based agents ( Yao et al., 2023 ) . The observed degradation reflects a systematic interaction-level phenomenon rather than isolated failures or prompt artifacts. Consequently, the use of thinking in user-engaged environments requires a rigorous understanding. To understand why thinking can be detrimental in these settings, we move beyond aggregate metrics and carefully analyze how thinking changes agent behavior during interaction. Our study unveils that enabling thinking consistently reduces information disclosure (i.e., proactively presenting environment observation to the user) across nearly all models. Instead of proactively disclosing pivotal information, thinking agents become more “introverted”, offering narrower and more selective information. This reduction in outward communication weakens active information exchange and, in interactive environments where progress depends on clarification through dialogue, can significantly hinder task completion. Through qualitative case studies, we further show how such omissions propagate through interaction: by failing to surface critical constraints or alternatives at key decision points, thinking agents inadvertently steer the trajectory toward failure. Our findings have direct implications for the design, deployment, and evaluation of LLM-based agents in user-engaged settings. Importantly, our study suggests that agent design should explicitly prioritize transparency, proactive information disclosure, and clarification over purely internal deliberation. To validate the practical benefits of our analysis, we further develop information-disclosure prompting and demonstrate empirically how it can improve performance across diverse model families, indicating that the observed introverted behavior is a correctable design choice rather than an inherent limitation of reasoning-capable models. More broadly, our results highlight the importance of evaluating reasoning mechanisms in realistic, user-engaged settings, as improvements observed on closed-world benchmarks may not reliably translate to interactive agent performance. We summarize our contributions below. 1. We conduct a comprehensive empirical study on the effect of mandatory thinking in user-engaged LLM agents across multiple models, benchmarks, and thinking instantiations. We observe an interesting phenomenon that thinking is not always beneficial, and can even be harmful, in interactive scenarios. 2. We provide a fine-grained behavioral analysis revealing how thinking makes LLM agents “introverted”, by discovering that thinking reduces response length and information disclosure to users, helping explain the observed performance degradation. 3. We propose an effective yet simple add-on prompting strategy that enhances information disclosure to boost agent performance, demonstrating the potential of information transparancy awareness in agent optimization. 2 Related Work User-engaged agent has become a significant category of modern LLM agents in both industrial use and academic research ( Clarke et al., 2022 ; Deshpande et al., 2025 ) . They communicate with the user via language response ( Qian et al., 2024 ) and interact with the environment via formatted action ( Yao et al., 2023 ) or tool calling ( OpenAI, 2025a ) to achieve the user’s goal. As their impact becomes broader, a sophisticated evaluation for them is increasingly crucial. Recent studies in this field mainly focus on specific tasks ( Yao et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2024 ) or limited running environments ( Lu et al., 2025 ; Rawles et al., 2025 ; Deng et al., 2024 ) , representing two perspectives of simulating realistic agent environments. In contrast, our work focuses on understanding how internal reasoning mechanisms influence agent-user interaction across diverse user-engaged scenarios, providing a behavior-level perspective that complements prior benchmark-driven studies. Test-time scaling through thinking is a milestone method to enable LLMs to handle complicated tasks ( Muennighoff et al., 2025 ; Wei et al., 2022 ; Sprague et al., 2025 ) . Regarding LLM agents, massive effort has been devoted to using thinking to enhance action planning ( Yao et al., 2023 ; Qiao et al., 2024 ) , learning from memories ( Shinn et al., 2023 ) , or improving tool calling ( Song et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2024 ; Wu et al., 2025a ) . Despite its early success, the effectiveness of thinking has recently been challenged ( Ghosal et al., 2025 ) . Recent works discovered that thinking length is sometimes negatively related to performance ( Yang et al., 2025 ; Wu et al., 2025b ; Levy et al., 2024 ) . Others found that LLMs can act like ‘System-1’ (quick, short) or ‘System-2’ (deliberate, long) thinkers according to different instantiations ( Sivaprasad et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025 ) . Meanwhile, Shen et al. (2025) found that thinking trades off the interaction of web agents, impacting goal achievement negatively. Our work complements these studies by analyzing the impact of test-time thinking on agent-user interaction in user-engaged scenarios, which is underexplored. 3 Preliminaries 3.1 User-Engaged Agent Tasks Figure 2: Overall performance of agents with or without thinking on Retail and Airline. We study user-engaged agents operating in partially observable environments ( Gao et al., 2025 ) , where the agent must interact with users and tools to uncover intent and task-relevant information to achieve a complex final goal, such as travel booking or item retail. At each turn t t , the agent policy π θ ​ ( a t | o t ) \pi_{\theta}(a_{t}|o_{t}) maps the current context (interaction history and tool outputs) to an action: either a natural language response or a structured tool call. Crucially, language responses act as environmental dynamics; they directly shape the user’s subsequent actions and the resulting trajectory. Task success thus depends on the agent’s ability to ask for clarification and disclose information to the user by aligning the interaction with the final goal. 3.2 Formulation of Agent’s Thinking Agent thinking can be viewed as an internal, user-invisible generation process that precedes action selection. Specifically, thinking does not alter the environment; rather, it serves as an intervention on the action sampling distribution. Given an observation o t o_{t} , a thinking agent first generates internal tokens τ t \tau_{t} , then samples an action a t ∼ π θ ( ⋅ | o t , τ t ) a_{t}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|o_{t},\tau_{t}) . We consider two common instantiations of this: Thinking-as-a-Function (TaaF) is designed for tool-calling agents, where thinking is implemented as a mandatory function call executed before any response or tool invocation. The prompt instruction for TaaF is shown in Appendix A.1 . Thinking-as-a-Prefix (TaaP) is designed for textual agents ( Nakano et al., 2021 ) , where thinking is elicited via a prompt prefix (e.g., “Thought:…”) and precedes the action generation. This setting follows standard ReAct-style prompting ( Yao et al., 2023 ) , shown in Appendix A.1 . 4 Evaluation of Thinking Agents In this section, we empirically evaluate whether enabling thinking improves the performance of LLM agents in user-engaged, multi-turn interaction scenarios. We comprehensively compare agents with and without thinking across multiple models, environments, and thinking instantiations. We describe the experimental setup in Sec. 4.1 and main observations in Sec. 4.2 . 4.1 Experimental Setup Models. We conduct a comprehensive evaluation of seven representative LLMs, spanning both proprietary and open-source categories. We select four proprietary models, GPT-5 ( OpenAI, 2025b ) , GPT-4.1 ( OpenAI, 2025d ) , GPT-4o ( OpenAI, 2024 ) , and Gemini-2.5-Pro ( Gemini Team, 2025 ) , based on their superior performance and widespread adoption in real-world agent scenarios. Additionally, we include three open-source models: DeepSeek-V3.1 ( DeepSeek, 2025 ) , gpt-oss-120b ( OpenAI, 2025c ) , and Qwen3-30B-A3B Instruct ( Qwen Team, 2025 ) . Evaluation Scenarios. To ensure comprehensive evaluation, we consider three representative user-engaged scenarios from established benchmarks: τ \tau -Retail and τ \tau -Airline from τ \tau -bench ( Yao et al., 2025 ) , and TS-Phone (i.e., MULTIPLE_USER_TURN) from ToolSandbox ( Lu et al., 2025 ) . Contrary to the common belief that explicit reasoning broadly improves agent behavior ( Yao et al., 2023 ) , we find that enabling thinking often degrades performance in user-engaged scenarios. Notably, all GPT-series models exhibit degraded performance, and several open-source models suffer substantial declines. For instance in Table 2 , the performance of GPT-5 drops by 6.09% on TS-Phone; the performance of Gemini-2.5-Pro drops by 37.00% on τ \tau -Retail; the performance of DeepSeek-V3.1 drops by 6.69% on τ \tau -Retail. This pattern is not specific to a particular benchmark or evaluation protocol. As shown in Table 2 and Table 6 , similar trend persists under different thinking instantiations (Thinking-as-a-Function and Thinking-as-a-Prefix). The effect across models, tasks, and metrics suggests that the observed degradation reflects a systematic interaction-level phenomenon. The observed performance degradation naturally leads to a deeper question: why does thinking harm agent performance in interactive settings? To answer this question, we conduct additional empirical analysis and methodological exploration in the following sections, aiming to uncover how thinking changes agent behavior at the interaction level. Figure 6: Average number of information disclosure per task of agents with or without thinking. 5 Empirical Analysis of Thought Effect In this section, we delve deep into understanding why thinking degrades the agent’s performance in user-engaged settings. Our analysis proceeds in three steps. First, we quantify how thinking affects output (Sec. 5.1 ). Second, we examine how reduced output manifests as diminished information disclosure using a fine-grained response taxonomy (Sec. 5.2 ). Finally, we present a qualitative case study illustrating how insufficient disclosure propagates into task failure (Sec. 5.3 ). 5.1 Thinking Reduces Output Scaling We begin by investigating the impact of thinking on output scaling by analyzing changes in response token length before and after enabling the thinking mechanism in agents. We perform a trajectory-level analysis on the Retail and Airline benchmarks. Specifically, we consider two metrics: (1) the average response length per trajectory and (2) the frequency of long responses within a trajectory, with at least 150 tokens. Details are available at Appendix A.4 . As illustrated in Figure 3 , there is a pronounced decline in response length across most LLMs when thinking is enabled. This pattern is further confirmed by paired statistical tests reported in Table 3 , which demonstrate a significant decrease in the number of long responses for the majority of models. For instance, DeepSeek-V3.1 produces an average of 1.24 long responses per trajectory without thinking, but drops sharply to 0.40 with thinking. These results suggest that thinking forces agents to generate more concise outputs. While brevity can be beneficial in some settings, in interactive scenarios, it may also reduce clarification and information exchange. To further investigate the implications of this reduced output, we conduct a semantic analysis of the responses. Blue text labels pivotal information disclosure that leads to task success. 5.2 Thinking Reduces Information Disclosure in Agent Responses To examine how reduced output length affects interaction quality, we introduce an atomic response taxonomy that decomposes each agent response into semantically indivisible units, referred to as atomic statements. Each atomic statement is categorized into one of two functional types: (1) information disclosure , which communicates the current world state or available options to users, and (2) user engagement request , which prompts the user for input or action. For example, as illustrated in Figure 5 , an airline agent’s response can be explicitly partitioned into six atomic statements: four instances of information disclosure and two user engagement requests. Maintaining sufficient information disclosure and engagement is indispensable for effective agent-user interaction. For the scalable analysis, we propose an autonomous taxonomy annotation pipeline that efficiently parses atomic responses and classifies them into categories (see Appendix A.5 ). We validate the reliability of our pipeline via human-in-the-loop annotation (see Appendix A.6 ). Using this taxonomy, we compare the frequency of information disclosure in the scenarios. We focus primarily on information disclosure as it provides the essential context and affordances required for meaningful user engagement, effectively serving as a proxy for the agent’s interactive capacity. As shown in Figure 6 , enabling thinking leads to a substantial and consistent reduction in information disclosure to users across nearly all models , spanning both proprietary and open-source architectures. These results suggest that thinking renders agents more “introverted”: rather than proactively summarizing observations or enumerating options, thinking agents tend to provide narrower, more selective information. As a result, this diminishes active information exchange with the user. In user-engaged scenarios, where the user’s intent is partially observable and must be clarified through interaction, this reduction in disclosure can significantly hinder task progress. 5.3 Case Study: Insufficient Information Disclosure Misleads the User To concretely illustrate how reduced information disclosure can lead to task failure, we conduct a qualitative case study across three scenarios. We first manually sample the cases where the thinking agent fails while the non-thinking agent succeeds. Subsequently, we perform a backtracking analysis of the failure and success propagation within the agent’s actions. Finally, we provide a trajectory comparison to demonstrate the specific impact of thinking on agent-user interaction. We consider a retail task scenario, e.g., a user wanting to return a skateboard, with a detailed task description provided in Figure 4 . The trajectories for the thinking and non-thinking agents are shown in Figure 7 , respectively (additional cases are presented in Appendix A.7 ). A critical decision point in this scenario hinges on whether the agent informs the user that an item they bought cannot be canceled individually due to order constraints. This requires a sufficient level of information disclosure, as conceptualized in Section 5.2 . For the agent with thinking (see the left of Figure 7 ), we observe that the internal monologue overlooks the specific constraints regarding item cancellation. This localized action planning curtails the information disclosure provided in the subsequent response, causing the agent to omit the necessary warning. Consequently, this lack of transparency misleads the user into making an incorrect decision, resulting in task failure. In contrast, the agent without the explicit thinking proactively discloses the cancellation constraint. This active communication alerts the user to the fact that cancelling the hose alone is infeasible, which in turn empowers the user to make a correct decision based on sufficient information. This case study demonstrates that the thinking may inadvertently lead to insufficient information disclosure, thereby leading to downstream user errors. 6 Discussion and Practical Implications Our findings have several important implications for the design, deployment, and evaluation of LLM-based agents in interactive settings. Information transparency can drive agents’ goal achievement. Our findings suggest that the next generation of user-engaged agents must move beyond raw reasoning power toward transparency-aware design. While current paradigms prioritize internal thinking, future agents must treat external interaction as a top priority of the task process. We demonstrate the potential of this direction by our preliminary experiments with Information Disclosure ( InfoDis ), an add-on prompt that simply instructing agents to prioritize informative transparency (see Appendix A.8 for technical details). As shown in Table 4 , we observed immediate and consistent performance gains across various model families GPT-4o (OpenAI), Gemini-1.5-Pro (Google), and DeepSeek-V3.1 (DeepSeek), such as a +4.00% increase in the τ \tau -Airline for DeepSeek-V3.1. The fact that such a lightweight prompting intervention yields such significant improvements across diverse model families signals a major optimization frontier. It suggests that “introverted” behavior by reasoning is not an inherent limitation, but a design gap that can be bridged. We argue that instilling transparency awareness into LLMs, whether through architectural shifts, supervised fine-tuning, or reinforcement learning, represents a potential lever for better agentic system design. This path promises a new class of agents that not only solve tasks in isolation, but actively manage user uncertainty through strategic disclosure and clarification. User-centric reasoning LLMs development. Our empirical analysis demonstrates a counterintuitive trade-off in user-engaged scenarios: thinking can hinder goal achievements by rendering agents more “introverted”. Our results suggest that the common thinking pattern of LLMs should be reconsidered in user-engaged scenarios. In existing settings, thinking is designed for complex but fully observed, single-turn tasks. Such a thinking pattern can suppress information disclosure and reduce exploratory communication, which is harmful to more general user-engaged scenarios. Therefore, developers should pursue new data and training strategies to guide LLMs to acquire more user-centric thinking patterns for agentic utility. Broader lessons for agent evaluation. Finally, our results caution against transferring intuitions from closed-world reasoning benchmarks directly to interactive agent deployments. While explicit thinking can improve performance in static tasks, it may introduce unintended side effects in dynamic, user-facing systems. For practitioners, this underscores the importance of validating reasoning techniques under realistic interaction conditions before deploying them in production agents. Through a comprehensive evaluation across seven representative models and multiple benchmarks, we uncovered a consistent serendipity: enforcing thinking before actions can degrade performance in user-engaged settings. Our analysis shows that this degradation arises from a systematic behavioral shift, where thinking shortens responses and reduces information disclosure, making agents more “introverted” and less effective at guiding users through underspecified tasks. Qualitative case studies further illustrate how such omissions propagate into task failures. To translate these insights into practical utility, we presented a simple information-disclosure prompting method, and showed that it can reliably recover and improve performance across model families. Overall, our results highlight the importance of evaluating reasoning mechanisms in realistic interactive environments and motivate interaction-aware agent design that balances internal deliberation with proactive communication. Limitations While our study provides a systematic analysis of how explicit reasoning affects agent behavior in user-engaged scenarios, we acknowledge several limitations that offer avenues for future research. First, our evaluation is centered on three representative user-engaged benchmarks that primarily represent task-oriented dialogues. Future work should explore whether the thinking effect persists in more open-ended or creative collaboration scenarios where the user’s intent is less structured. Moreover, our behavioral analyses rely on automated response taxonomy and thought categorization pipelines supported by large language models, with human validation. While we observe strong agreement between model-based and human annotations, subtle categorization errors may remain, particularly for borderline cases involving implicit disclosure or nuanced user engagement. Ethical Considerations This study presents an empirical analysis of the “thinking effect” within user-engaged agents. The methodology and findings detailed herein are intended to advance the research and practical application of LLM agents, providing an empirical foundation and reference for future development in the field. Furthermore, we remain committed to transparency and reproducibility; all data resources and models utilized in this research are derived from publicly available sources and are used in accordance with their respective licensing agreements. We anticipate no significant foreseeable negative social impacts resulting from this work. A.3 Analysis of Agent Thought Contents Quantitative analysis on agent thoughts is inherently challenging due to their linguistic complexity and their implicit influence on task trajectories. To address this, we propose a hierarchical thought taxonomy informed by three key observations: (1) complex agent thoughts can be decomposed into a sequence of simpler, atomic units; (2) each atomic thought serves either as action planning or state perception; and (3) the subject of an atomic thought is either the user or the environment. Based on these principles, we established a two-level hierarchical classification system. An example showing all thougt categories is shown in Figure 8 . For our empirical analysis, we randomly sampled 20% of the trajectories from our dataset and employed GPT-4.1 to decompose and categorize the agent thoughts accordingly. The distribution of this taxonomy is illustrated in Figure 9 , where yellow segments represent action planning (including user-interactive actions and tool-calling actions) and blue segments represent state perception (including user intention confirmation and database observation summarization). Our visualization reveals two primary findings. First, action planning dominates the thought processes of many agents, particularly within the GPT series. In these models, over half of the generated thoughts focus on planning future actions based on existing observations. While such proactive planning is essential for complex reasoning, it may be suboptimal in user-engaged scenarios where current observations are often insufficient for task completion without further user clarification. Second, the specific instantiation of the "thinking" process significantly shifts thought content. For example, the proportion of tool-calling thoughts in GPT-5 increases from 44.4% to 59.5% when transitioning from Thinking-as-a-Function (TaaF) to Thinking-as-a-Prefix (TaaP) framework. This suggests that thinking patterns are highly sensitive to framework design and prompt instructions. Ultimately, while our taxonomy effectively characterizes agent thinking patterns, it does not directly measure their causal impact on subsequent actions; these effects are further explored through our analysis of response lengths, action taxonomies, and qualitative case studies. A.5 Detailed Experiment Setup of Response Taxonomy Considering efficiency and accuracy, we utilize the strong natural language understanding and few-shot learning abilities of proprietary LLMs to automatically annotate response taxonomy for trajectory data. The few-shot prompt instruction is shown in Figure 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 , and 14 . In practice, to ensure more accurate annotation, we provide a fine-grained two-level hierarchical taxonomy in the LLM prompt instruction. The two-level taxonomy has a clearer definition for the LLM to annotate sentences. Specifically, for information disclosure , we propose the observation summarization and choice enumeration . For user engagement request , we propose the close-ended inquiry and open-ended inquiry . The definition of these categories is presented in Figure 11 . EXAMPLE : " Is there a specific type of t - shirt you ’ re looking for " - 2.2 Open - ended inquiry : The agent ’ s atomic statement requires the user to take action ( s ) from an unlimited space . Although sometimes the semantic of the statement depends on the context , but the user action space is always unlimited . EAMPLE : " Would you prefer to look at other products ?" A.6 Human-in-the-loop Validation of Response Taxonomy To validate the effectiveness of the automatic response taxonomy pipeline, we conduct a human-in-the-loop experiment of response taxonomy annotation. Ideally, if the automatic pipeline is valid, then we could observe a similar number of response categories for human annotation and model annotation. Specifically, we select approximately 1,060 atomic responses from 20 trajectories (10 trajectories from τ \tau -Retail and 10 trajectories from τ \tau -Airline, with DeepSeek-V3.1 as a target agent of investigation). For each scenario, half of the trajectories are from agents without thinking, while the other half are from agents with thinking. Next, we do the manual validation based on the random assignment criteria. As shown in Table 7 , the human-in-the-loop validation result demonstrates an excellent consistency of annotation between the human expert and GPT-4.1. For both categories, we observe a consistent drop in frequency per trajectory, as the frequency drops from 47.1 to 37.8 with the human expert’s annotation. This result demonstrates the effectiveness of use the automatic pipeline for efficient and reliable annotation in this study. Also, we observe that the human-in-the-loop annotation is time-consuming, taking 2h 10min to complete for 20 trajectories. On average, each trajectory takes 6 min 30 s for a human expert to annotate. A.7 Other Cases of Agent Trajectories In the case study, we also study task cases in τ \tau -Airline and TS-Phone, respectively. Both scenarios are marked by the partially observed environment and dynamic user interaction. Case study of τ \tau -Airline. Figure 16 , 17 and 18 show a summary of the task case, trajectory snapshots of the agent with thinking and the agent without thinking, respectively. The key challenge of this task is that the user’s initial returning flight from IAH to LAS has already been nonstop, but the user doesn’t remember. Therefore, the agent needs to disclose this information to the user to prevent unnecessary flight bookings. As shown in Figure 17 , although the thinking agent found available non-stop flights for both outbound and return, it fails to disclose existing flight booking information to the user. This misleads the user to unnecessarily update the return flight to HAT131, causing task failure. Case study of TS-Phone. Figure 19 presents the case of TS-Phone. The key challenge of this task lies in the semantic gap between the ground truth (the time length until Christmas day) and the pre-given user initial request (what is the date of Christmas day). The agent must actively interact with the user to propel the user to express the accurate intention. As shown in Figure 19 , the agent with thinking indeed accurately answers the exact date of Christmas Day. However, it does not disclose any other information or any requests to the user. In practice, this introverted response pattern can reduce the interaction intention of the user, leading to task failure. Differently, the non-thinking agent not only accurately answers the date of Christmas Day, but also discloses its current situation and requests. e.g., it cannot look up the exact date at the moment because the Wi-Fi is disabled. Semantically, this more active response pattern encourages the user to actively respond to the agent, too, as shown in the difference between the tone of the user in the two trajectories. A.8 Details of InfoDis Experiment Vanilla Prompting. The vanilla prompt is the initial system message to tool-calling agents. For each scenario, the vanilla prompt consists of a demonstration of the sceanrio, and the task policy. The task policy regulates the rules and constraints of agent actions in different situations. InfoDis Prompting. The information disclosure (InfoDis) prompting template is shown in Figure 15 . To ensure fairness, we do not include any task-specific few-shot examples in the template. In practice, the InfoDis prompting is added to the end of the task policy prompt (vanilla prompt) of agents. Therefore, InfoDis is implemented as an add-on of user-engaged agents.
